paths.name: SOC Analyst
paths.summary: You watch for attacks as they happen, separate real threats from noise and act fast when something is wrong. It's one of the most common first jobs in cybersecurity.
day: Review security alerts and decide which ones are real
Look into suspicious sign-ins and programs
Hand real incidents to responders with clear notes
start: Learn what normal Windows and Linux logs look like
Practise triage on free blue-team challenges

paths.name: Digital Forensics & Incident Response
paths.summary: You rebuild exactly what happened from the clues left behind, contain the damage and make sure the attacker is really gone.
day: Build timelines from logs, disks and memory
Lock down compromised computers and accounts
Write up what happened and how to stop it next time
start: Practise reading logs and building a timeline

paths.name: Malware Analyst
paths.tagline: The one who takes threats apart
paths.summary: You study suspicious programs in a safe lab to learn what they do and how they hide, then turn that into detections that protect everyone.
day: Run suspicious files in an isolated sandbox
Work out what a program really does
Write detection rules and share what you found
start: Set up a safe, isolated practice lab
Learn the basics of static and dynamic analysis

paths.name: OSINT & Threat Intelligence
paths.summary: You find answers hiding in plain sight. Public websites, photos and records become intelligence that tells defenders who is coming and how.
day: Investigate websites, accounts and online infrastructure
Track scam and attack campaigns over time
Turn findings into clear, careful reports
start: Learn the OSINT cycle and how to stay ethical
Practise verifying photos, places and websites

paths.name: Penetration Tester
paths.summary: With written permission, you test systems the way a real attacker would, then show the owners exactly how to fix every weakness you found.
day: Map what a system exposes to the internet
Test websites and networks for weaknesses, with permission
Write reports developers can act on
start: Get fluent on the Linux command line
Learn the most common web weaknesses (the OWASP Top 10)

paths.name: Cloud & Security Engineering
paths.summary: You design and run the systems everything else depends on, and build security in from the start: access, configuration, automation and monitoring.
day: Set up servers and cloud services securely
Automate checks so mistakes get caught early
Decide who can access what
start: Learn how networks and the cloud fit together
Practise Linux permissions and least privilege

paths.name: Governance, Risk & Compliance
paths.summary: You make security work for the whole organisation: the policies, risk decisions and plans that stop problems before they start.
day: Assess risks and recommend sensible fixes
Check the organisation against frameworks like NIST
Explain security to people outside IT
start: Read the NIST Cybersecurity Framework overview
Practise explaining a technical risk in plain words

levels.step: Start with the basics of how computers and networks work. Keep our Glossary open and don't worry about jargon yet.

levels.a: I use computers a lot, but I've never worked in IT
levels.step: Get comfortable with the command line first. Shell quest is a gentle way in.

levels.a: I work or study in IT
levels.step: Turn your IT experience into security experience: ask to help with security tasks at work and write down what you learn.
Use your coding: build small scripts that automate a security task, and share them on GitHub.

questions.sub: No wrong answers. This only changes your first steps.

options.a: I'm completely new to tech
I use computers a lot, but I've never worked in IT
I work or study in IT
I can already write code

questions.q: Which kind of puzzle pulls you in?

options.a: A mystery: piecing together what happened
A lock: finding the way in
A machine: taking something apart to see how it works
A system: making something run safely for everyone

questions.q: Which mystery would you rather solve?

options.a: Who is behind a fake online shop, using only public information
How someone got into a company, from the clues they left
Which of today's thousand security alerts is the real attack

questions.q: Where would you look for the way in?

options.a: A website's login page and forms
The people: would someone fall for a fake email?
A strange program: what is it really doing?

questions.q: What would you most like to take apart?

options.a: A suspicious program, safely, to see what it does
A whole network, to see how the pieces connect
A hard drive, to recover what someone deleted
Setting up cloud servers that are secure from day one
Deciding who gets access to what, and why
Planning what everyone does when something goes wrong

questions.q: How do you like your work to feel?

options.a: Fast and busy, with a team around me
Calm and deep, one hard problem at a time
Varied, with a new project every few weeks
Organised, with plans and people to work with

questions.sub: All three are defence. Breaking in is always done with permission, to find weaknesses first.

options.a: Breaking in, so I can show where it's weak
Protecting, so nothing gets in
Investigating, after something already got in

questions.q: It's 2 a.m. and something is going wrong. How do you feel?

options.a: Let me at it. I want to be the one who answers
I'd rather study it calmly in the morning
I'd rather have stopped it from happening at all

questions.q: At the end of a job, what would make you proudest?

options.a: A clear timeline of exactly what happened
A list of weak spots, each with how to fix it
A report that reveals who is behind an attack
Knowing nothing got past me today
A system that just works, safely, for everyone

questions.q: How do you feel about learning to code?

options.a: Excited. I want to build things
Happy to learn small scripts
I'd rather focus on other skills

questions.q: How do you feel about explaining tech to people who aren't technical?

options.a: I enjoy it, even presenting to bosses
Fine now and then
I'd rather let my work speak for itself
A search engine and a map
A record of everything that happened on a computer
A safe sandbox to run something suspicious
A checklist of what every system should have
A dashboard full of cloud servers

questions.q: Would you rather go wide or deep?

options.a: Wide: lots of different things every day
Deep: become the expert in one hard thing

questions.q: You get a shiny new app or gadget. What do you wonder first?

options.a: How could someone misuse this?
What is it collecting about me?
How is it built and run behind the scenes?
